title: PyTorch Autograd Cheatsheet
name: PyTorch Autograd Cheatsheet
description: A production-oriented reference for PyTorch autograd gradient tracking, backward passes, inspection, graph control, hooks, inference mode, and custom autograd.

sections.title: Gradient Tracking
sections.description: Control whether operations compute and trace gradients for leaf parameters and intermediate variables.

sections.title: Backward Pass
sections.description: Compute vector-Jacobian products or compute gradients with respect to leaf tensors using backward, autograd.backward, and autograd.grad.

sections.title: Gradient Inspection
sections.description: Access, modify, and zero accumulated gradients using .grad, .grad.zero_, and .retain_grad.

sections.title: Graph Control
sections.description: Retain computation graphs, enable higher-order gradients, and detect numerical anomalies during backward propagation.

sections.title: Hooks
sections.description: Register custom callback hooks on tensors and modules during forward and backward passes.

sections.title: Inference Mode
sections.description: Disable gradient computation and view tracking for high-performance evaluation and inference using no_grad and inference_mode.

sections.title: Custom Autograd
sections.description: Define custom autograd functions and validate computed analytical gradients using finite-difference checks.

entries.trigger: Use this when initializing leaf tensors or input data that require automatic differentiation during backpropagation.
entries.snippet:
import torch

# Initialize leaf tensor with gradient tracking enabled
weights = torch.randn(4, 4, requires_grad=True)

# Compute intermediate tensor and loss
output = weights.pow(2).sum()
output.backward()

print(f"Requires grad: {weights.requires_grad}")
print(f"Gradient shape: {weights.grad.shape}")
entries.minimal_notes: Only floating point and complex tensor dtypes can require gradients, while integer or boolean tensors raise a RuntimeError. Gradient tracking applies transitively to all non-leaf tensors created downstream from tracked inputs.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** RuntimeError: Only Tensors of floating point and complex dtype can require gradients.

**Cause:** Passing integer or boolean dtype tensors into operations expecting requires_grad=True.

**Quick Fix:** Cast the tensor to floating point using .float() or .double() before setting requires_grad=True.

entries.trigger: Use this when freezing model parameters or detaching specific parameters in-place during fine-tuning or transfer learning.
entries.snippet:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Initialize a standard linear layer
layer = nn.Linear(10, 5)

# Freeze layer parameters in-place to prevent gradient computation
for param in layer.parameters():
    param.requires_grad_(False)

x = torch.randn(2, 10)
out = layer(x)
print(f"Output requires grad: {out.requires_grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: The trailing underscore indicates an in-place mutation of the tensor's state. You cannot call requires_grad_(False) on a non-leaf tensor that was generated within a computation graph.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** RuntimeError: you can only change requires_grad flags of leaf variables.

**Cause:** Calling .requires_grad_() on an intermediate tensor generated by upstream operations.

**Quick Fix:** Call .detach() on the intermediate tensor first before modifying gradient settings.

entries.trigger: Use this when extracting a tensor from the computation graph to stop gradient propagation without copying data.
entries.snippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(3, 3, requires_grad=True)
y = x * 2

# Detach y from computation graph; detached tensor shares underlying storage
y_detached = y.detach()
loss = y_detached.sum()

print(f"y_detached requires_grad: {y_detached.requires_grad}")
print(f"Shares storage: {y_detached.data_ptr() == y.data_ptr()}")
entries.minimal_notes: detach() returns a new view tensor that shares memory with the original tensor but has no gradient history. In-place modification of a detached tensor will affect the original tensor and trigger autograd errors if used in backward passes.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** RuntimeError: one of the variables needed for gradient computation has been modified by an inplace operation.

**Cause:** Modifying a detached tensor in-place while its parent tensor is required for autograd backward pass.

**Quick Fix:** Use .clone().detach() instead of .detach() when you plan to modify the detached data in-place.

entries.trigger: Use this to locally re-enable gradient calculation inside a torch.no_grad() or torch.inference_mode() block.
entries.snippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(2, 2, requires_grad=True)

with torch.no_grad():
    # Gradients disabled here
    intermediate = x * 2
    
    with torch.enable_grad():
        # Gradients re-enabled locally for fine-tuning or adversarial steps
        y = intermediate * 3
        loss = y.sum()
        loss.backward()

print(f"Gradient on x: {x.grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: torch.enable_grad can be used as a context manager or decorator to enforce gradient calculation. It operates thread-locally and does not impact autograd tracking in other running threads.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** Tensor.grad remains None after calling .backward().

**Cause:** Creating input tensors inside torch.no_grad() before entering torch.enable_grad(), causing intermediate tensors to lack graph connectivity.

**Quick Fix:** Ensure input tensors have requires_grad=True prior to entering the gradient-tracked section.

entries.trigger: Use this to trigger automatic backpropagation from a scalar loss tensor to compute gradients for all leaf parameters.
entries.snippet:
import torch

weights = torch.randn(3, 3, requires_grad=True)
inputs = torch.randn(3, 3)

# Forward pass computing scalar loss
loss = (weights @ inputs).sum()

# Compute gradients with respect to leaf tensors
loss.backward()

print(f"Calculated gradient:\n{weights.grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: If calling backward() on a non-scalar tensor, you must supply a gradient argument matching the tensor shape. Calling backward() frees graph buffers unless retain_graph=True is specified.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** RuntimeError: grad can be implicitly created only for scalar outputs.

**Cause:** Calling .backward() without arguments on a non-scalar tensor.

**Quick Fix:** Pass a matching weighting tensor, e.g. loss.backward(torch.ones_like(loss)), or reduce the tensor to a scalar using .sum().

entries.trigger: Use this to compute vector-Jacobian products across multiple output tensors or customized gradient targets simultaneously.
entries.snippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(3, requires_grad=True)
y = x * 2
z = x * 3

# Compute sum of vector-Jacobian products for multiple root outputs
grad_tensors = [torch.ones_like(y), torch.ones_like(z)]
torch.autograd.backward([y, z], grad_tensors=grad_tensors)

print(f"Accumulated gradient on x: {x.grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: torch.autograd.backward accumulates gradients directly into .grad attributes of specified graph leaves. The lengths of tensors and grad_tensors must match exactly unless output elements are scalar.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** RuntimeError: Mismatch in length of tensors and grad_tensors.

**Cause:** Passing a list of output tensors to torch.autograd.backward with a non-matching number of gradient weight tensors.

**Quick Fix:** Provide a matching grad_tensors list containing one tensor per output tensor.

entries.trigger: Use this when you need direct gradient values without mutating .grad attributes on model leaf tensors.
entries.snippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(3, requires_grad=True)
y = (x ** 2).sum()

# Compute gradient directly without populating x.grad
grads = torch.autograd.grad(outputs=y, inputs=x)

print(f"Direct gradient tuple: {grads[0]}")
print(f"x.grad remains None: {x.grad is None}")
entries.minimal_notes: torch.autograd.grad returns a tuple of gradients corresponding to the inputs tuple. Set allow_unused=True if some input tensors do not participate in the output computation.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** RuntimeError: One of the differentiated Tensors appears to not have been used in the graph.

**Cause:** Passing an input tensor to inputs that was not involved in generating outputs.

**Quick Fix:** Pass allow_unused=True to torch.autograd.grad to receive None for unused inputs.

entries.trigger: Use this to inspect or manipulate accumulated gradient values stored on leaf tensors after a backward pass.
entries.snippet:
import torch

w = torch.tensor([2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
loss = (w ** 2).sum()
loss.backward()

# Access accumulated gradients
gradient = w.grad
print(f"Accessing .grad: {gradient}")

# Safe in-place modification or gradient clipping inspection
print(f"Gradient norm: {torch.norm(w.grad)}")
entries.minimal_notes: The .grad attribute is None by default until backward() is executed. Gradients accumulate iteratively on subsequent backward() calls unless reset to zero or set to None.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'shape' or unexpected gradient accumulation.

**Cause:** Accessing .grad before calling backward(), or failing to zero .grad between training steps.

**Quick Fix:** Check if tensor.grad is not None: or clear gradients using optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True).

entries.trigger: Use this before every backpropagation pass to clear accumulated gradients from previous optimization steps.
entries.snippet:
import torch

w = torch.randn(2, 2, requires_grad=True)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([w], lr=0.01)

# Forward and backward step
(w * 2).sum().backward()

# Reset gradients to None for lower memory footprint and better performance
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

print(f"w.grad after zero_grad: {w.grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: Passing set_to_none=True to optimizer.zero_grad() frees memory allocations instead of writing zero tensors. Setting .grad = None improves execution speed and reduces memory overhead during training loops.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** Model gradients accumulate unintentionally, causing exploding gradients across batch iterations.

**Cause:** Forgetting to call optimizer.zero_grad() prior to executing loss.backward().

**Quick Fix:** Always place optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) before loss.backward() in the training step.

entries.trigger: Use this to inspect or extract gradients for non-leaf intermediate tensors during backward execution.
entries.snippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(3, requires_grad=True)
y = x * 2

# Request autograd to populate .grad on intermediate tensor y
y.retain_grad()

z = y.pow(2).sum()
z.backward()

print(f"Intermediate y.grad: {y.grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: By default, autograd discards non-leaf tensor gradients after backward pass completion to save memory. Calling retain_grad() must occur before backward() is invoked.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** Intermediate tensor .grad attribute remains None after backward().

**Cause:** Inspecting intermediate .grad without calling .retain_grad() prior to backpropagation.

**Quick Fix:** Call intermediate_tensor.retain_grad() immediately after its creation in the forward pass.

entries.trigger: Use this when you need to execute multiple backward passes through the same computation graph, such as in multi-task loss optimization.
entries.snippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(2, 2, requires_grad=True)
shared = x * 3

loss1 = shared.sum()
loss2 = shared.pow(2).sum()

# First backward pass retains graph for second backward
loss1.backward(retain_graph=True)
loss2.backward()

print(f"Accumulated gradients on x: {x.grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: retain_graph=True prevents autograd from freeing intermediate activation buffers after backpropagation. Holding graph buffers increases peak GPU memory usage significantly across iterations.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** RuntimeError: Trying to backward through the graph a second time (or directly access saved variables).

**Cause:** Calling backward() multiple times on a graph without setting retain_graph=True on earlier calls.

**Quick Fix:** Set retain_graph=True on all backward() calls except the final one.

entries.trigger: Use this to construct a graph of derivative operations for computing second-order or higher-order derivatives.
entries.snippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(1, requires_grad=True)
y = x ** 3

# Compute first derivative while creating computation graph for second derivative
first_grad = torch.autograd.grad(outputs=y, inputs=x, create_graph=True)[0]

# Compute second derivative (d2y/dx2 = 6x)
second_grad = torch.autograd.grad(outputs=first_grad, inputs=x)[0]

print(f"First derivative: {first_grad}")
print(f"Second derivative: {second_grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: Setting create_graph=True automatically implies retain_graph=True. Higher-order gradient tracking maintains extended graph histories, which increases memory consumption.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** GPU memory leaks when implementing second-order methods or gradient penalty loss functions.

**Cause:** Forgetting to detach higher-order gradient outputs before storing them in logs or metric accumulators.

**Quick Fix:** Call .detach() on scalar metrics computed from create_graph=True flows before logging.

entries.trigger: Use this to locate the exact forward operation that caused NaN or Inf values during backward propagation.
entries.snippet:
import torch

# Enable anomaly detection context manager
with torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True):
    x = torch.tensor([0.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)
    # Division by zero causes NaN in forward/backward
    y = torch.sqrt(x)
    loss = y.sum()
    
    try:
        loss.backward()
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"Anomaly detected successfully: {e}")
entries.minimal_notes: Anomaly detection incurs significant CPU and GPU runtime performance overhead. Enable it strictly while debugging numerical stability issues and keep it disabled in production training.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** Drastic reduction in training throughput across training runs.

**Cause:** Leaving torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True) active during standard production training.

**Quick Fix:** Wrap anomaly detection inside temporary debugging contexts or conditional flags only.

entries.trigger: Use this to inspect, modify, or clip gradients of specific tensors inline during the backward pass.
entries.snippet:
import torch

x = torch.randn(3, requires_grad=True)
y = x * 5

# Register hook to double gradient of tensor y during backward pass
handle = y.register_hook(lambda grad: grad * 2.0)

loss = y.sum()
loss.backward()

print(f"Modified gradient on x: {x.grad}")
handle.remove()  # Cleanup hook
entries.minimal_notes: The hook function must match hook(grad) -> Tensor or None. Returning a new tensor modifies the gradient flowing backward, while returning None leaves it unchanged.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** RuntimeError or unintended gradient transformations persisting across epochs.

**Cause:** Forgetting to store and invoke handle.remove() when temporary gradient inspection is complete.

**Quick Fix:** Always store the handle returned by register_hook and call handle.remove() when done.

entries.trigger: Use this to inspect intermediate layer feature maps or perform activations logging without modifying module code.
entries.snippet:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Linear(10, 5)
activations = {}

def hook_fn(module, input, output):
    activations['linear_out'] = output.detach()

# Register hook on target module
handle = model.register_forward_hook(hook_fn)

x = torch.randn(2, 10)
_ = model(x)

print(f"Captured activation shape: {activations['linear_out'].shape}")
handle.remove()
entries.minimal_notes: The hook signature is hook(module, input, output) -> None or modified output. Outputs attached directly without .detach() can accidentally retain computation graphs and cause memory leaks.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** Memory leak accumulating GPU memory over time during evaluation or inference.

**Cause:** Storing raw output tensors inside external lists/dicts without detaching them from the autograd graph.

**Quick Fix:** Always extract activations using output.detach() inside forward hook callables.

entries.trigger: Use this to monitor or modify input and output gradients passing through an entire nn.Module during backpropagation.
entries.snippet:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

layer = nn.Linear(5, 2)

def backward_hook(module, grad_input, grad_output):
    print(f"Grad output shape: {grad_output[0].shape}")
    print(f"Grad input shape: {grad_input[0].shape}")

# Register full backward hook on module
handle = layer.register_full_backward_hook(backward_hook)

x = torch.randn(2, 5, requires_grad=True)
out = layer(x).sum()
out.backward()

handle.remove()
entries.minimal_notes: The hook signature is hook(module, grad_input, grad_output). Arguments grad_input and grad_output are tuples corresponding to input and output positional arguments.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** Deprecation warnings or unexpected runtime errors when using register_backward_hook.

**Cause:** Using legacy register_backward_hook which fails on complex modules with multiple inputs/outputs.

**Quick Fix:** Use register_full_backward_hook for reliable module-level backward gradient inspection.

entries.trigger: Use this during evaluation, validation, or inference to disable autograd tracking and save GPU memory.
entries.snippet:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Linear(10, 2)
model.eval()

x = torch.randn(4, 10)

# Disable gradient calculation for evaluation pass
with torch.no_grad():
    predictions = model(x)

print(f"Predictions require grad: {predictions.requires_grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: torch.no_grad() disables gradient computation but preserves view tracking and version counter increments. It can be used as both a context manager and a function decorator.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** Excessive GPU memory usage and slower throughput during validation loops.

**Cause:** Omitting with torch.no_grad(): during evaluation passes, building unused computation graphs.

**Quick Fix:** Wrap validation and testing forward passes inside a with torch.no_grad(): context block.

entries.trigger: Use this for production model deployment and inference loops to achieve maximum runtime speedup and lowest memory footprint.
entries.snippet:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Linear(8, 4)
model.eval()

x = torch.randn(2, 8)

# Preferred high-performance context for production inference
with torch.inference_mode():
    output = model(x)

print(f"Inference output shape: {output.shape}")
print(f"Requires grad: {output.requires_grad}")
entries.minimal_notes: torch.inference_mode() is a faster drop-in replacement for torch.no_grad() that disables view tracking and version counter checks. Tensors created inside inference mode cannot be used in subsequent autograd computations.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** RuntimeError: Inference tensors do not track version counter or cannot be used in autograd.

**Cause:** Attempting to mutate or pass a tensor generated within inference_mode into an autograd-tracked region.

**Quick Fix:** Use torch.no_grad() instead if created tensors must later interact with gradient-tracked operations.

entries.trigger: Use this when implementing custom forward operations or custom backward gradient formulas not natively supported by PyTorch.
entries.minimal_notes: Always invoke custom functions via Function.apply(*inputs) rather than calling forward() directly. Use ctx.save_for_backward(*tensors) to stash intermediate tensors required during backward computation.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** Memory leaks or incorrect autograd graph construction when calling custom autograd functions.

**Cause:** Calling CubeFunction.forward(x) directly instead of CubeFunction.apply(x).

**Quick Fix:** Always use CustomFunction.apply(...) to execute forward and register the backward pass.

entries.trigger: Use this in unit tests to numerically verify analytical gradients computed by custom torch.autograd.Function implementations.
entries.minimal_notes: gradcheck compares finite-difference numerical gradients against analytical backward gradients. Test tensors must use torch.float64 precision to avoid false test failures due to floating-point truncation errors.
entries.common_bug:
**Issue:** GradcheckError or false precision failure during gradient validation tests.

**Cause:** Passing default float32 tensors into gradcheck instead of double-precision float64 tensors.

**Quick Fix:** Initialize test tensors with dtype=torch.float64 and requires_grad=True.
